article_title: Executive Summary: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity
citation: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/
title: Identify and mitigate bias in AI to keep educational AI compatible with digital equity commitments
description: The brief argues that because AI automates educational processes based on associations found in data, and "the associations in existing data often contain bias," automations built on biased associations could increase unfair and unlawful discrimination. Identifying and mitigating bias is therefore essential to using AI in ways compatible with commitments to Digital Equity, as discussed in the US Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights.
requirements: Identification and mitigation of bias in the data associations underlying AI automations
constraints: Grounded in the US Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights
target_learners: all students
educational leaders
target_learning_goals: fair and equitable use of AI in education
examples: The brief links bias mitigation to the United States Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights as a digital equity commitment
key_sources: A Look at AI Literacy, and AI and Digital Equity. (2024). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org/2024/02/20/how-ai-for-education-can-address-digital-equity/

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Identify the specifics of the problem behavior and the conditions that prompt and reinforce it before intervening
description: Before selecting an intervention, teachers should concretely describe the problem behavior and its effect on learning, observe and record its frequency and context, and identify its antecedents and consequences. The guide recommends that "teachers carefully observe the conditions in which the problem behavior of an individual student is likely to occur and not occur", then use that information to tailor intervention strategies to the individual student within the classroom context. This analytic step is rated moderate evidence and underlies functional behavioral assessment practice.
requirements: Concretely describe the behavior problem and its effect on learning
Observe and record the frequency and context of the problem behavior over a few days to a week until clear patterns emerge
Identify what prompts and reinforces the problem behavior
constraints: The panel does not suggest that general education teachers conduct formal functional behavioral assessments and analyses on their own
Much of the supporting evidence comes from students with school-identified emotional and behavioral disabilities
target_learners: Elementary general education students (K-5) with persistent problem behaviors
target_learning_goals: Reducing inappropriate classroom behavior that impedes learning
examples: Concrete descriptions the guide offers include a student who blurts out answers without raising his hand during whole-class instruction and a student who frequently leaves her seat without permission during small-group instruction.
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: High School Graduation and College Readiness Indicator Systems
citation: Allensworth, E.M., Nagaoka, J., & Johnson, D.W. (2018). High school graduation and college readiness indicator systems: What we know, what we need to know. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://ncs.uchicago.edu/freshman-on-track-toolkit
title: Choose indicators that are predictive, usable, available in real time, causally linked to attainment, and malleable through school practices
description: The report proposes five ideal properties of indicators, each building on the prior: predictiveness, usability and clarity, real-time/right-time availability, direct causal linkage to educational attainment, and malleability. It states that "Indicators that are known to be malleable through specific practices—and that are strongly and causally linked to educational attainment—provide the greatest opportunity for improving students' outcomes." The properties are offered as selection criteria for deciding which indicators should be the focus of an early warning or college readiness indicator system.
requirements: The decision of which indicators to focus on should be shaped by the plan for how the indicators will be used; indicators are not effective if practitioners do not have strategies to act on them
Indicators must be calculable in a timely way and understandable, since some indicators are difficult to calculate or confusing and difficult to use
constraints: The review states there is insufficient research to evaluate any of the indicators being used along all of these dimensions

The review warns that predictive analytics approaches, while highly predictive, risk replicating and reinforcing previous inequitable or discriminatory patterns because models are based on historical data
target_learners: High school students
Middle grades students
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College readiness
examples: The review contrasts ninth-grade GPA, which predicted Chicago graduation with 80 percent accuracy, against eighth-grade test scores and background characteristics at 65 percent accuracy
The review notes educators may benefit from multiple indicators if they provide complementary types of information that aid intervention efforts
key_sources: Allensworth, E.M., Nagaoka, J., & Johnson, D.W. (2018). High school graduation and college readiness indicator systems: What we know, what we need to know. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://ncs.uchicago.edu/freshman-on-track-toolkit

article_title: Creating Identity-Safe Schools and Classrooms
citation: Hernández, L. E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Creating identity-safe schools and classrooms. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/165.102
title: Identity safety framework: four practice areas that counteract social identity threat in schools
description: The report organizes identity-safe schooling around four research-backed practice areas: trusting relationships and interpersonal connection; caring, consistent, purposeful communities; restorative practices; and teaching that promotes "understanding, student voice, student responsibility" plus cultivating "diversity as a resource for teaching." It rests on the science-of-learning premise that social, emotional, and cognitive experiences are intertwined, so threat reduction and belonging are preconditions for achievement. The framework is offered as the antidote to stereotype threat.
requirements: Educators appreciate and understand students' experiences, assets, and backgrounds
Consistent routines and structures (advisories, looping, community meetings) that let positive connections flourish
constraints: The report frames these as supports for students facing social identity threat from stigma based on race, ethnicity, gender identity, language, immigration status, disability, or other features
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those from minoritized or stigmatized groups
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging and membership in school
Student achievement and engagement
Reduced effects of stereotype threat
key_sources: Hernández, L. E., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2022). Creating identity-safe schools and classrooms. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/165.102

article_title: A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling
citation: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://edtrust.org
title: Ideal pathways system: intentional, supported trajectories with consistent guidance from middle school through adulthood
description: The brief defines pathways as "the full universe of intentional and supported trajectories that every learner understands and participates in as they move from adolescence through adulthood." The framework spans CTE, work-based learning including internships and apprenticeships, early postsecondary opportunities (advanced coursework, AP, IB, dual enrollment, early college), and postsecondary programs leading to industry-recognized credentials or degrees. Learners receive "consistent, knowledgeable guidance, beginning in middle school, from well-qualified counselors and navigators" and are supported over time to find, experience, and move among pathways aligned with their desired social, economic, and personal outcomes.
requirements: Well-qualified counselors and navigators with knowledge of the full range of options and capacity to connect students to opportunities
Guidance beginning in middle school and continuing through transitions
constraints: The current patchwork of programs and funding streams is described as inadequate to address the scale and urgency of the challenge
target_learners: Students ages 16-24, particularly low-income, first-generation students and students of color
target_learning_goals: College and career navigation and informed pathway choice
examples: The brief's convening of national partners in fall 2023 produced this collective definition to guide federal policy recommendations
key_sources: Rebeca Shackleford and Kristen Hengtgen. (2024). A Vision for Equitable Pathways: Enhancing Support and Innovation in College and Career Counseling. EdTrust/All4Ed. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED670956

article_title: Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government
citation: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2
title: Identity-protective cognition thesis (ICT)
description: ICT is the article's explanatory framework for persistent public conflict over societal risks. It "treats cultural conflict as disabling the faculties that members of the public use to make sense of decision-relevant science". On this account, people with greater reasoning skill are not more accurate on identity-charged data; instead they "use their quantitative-reasoning capacity selectively to conform their interpretation of the data to the result most consistent with their political outlooks". The experiment's finding that polarization increased with numeracy was read as supporting this thesis over the science comprehension thesis.
requirements: A dataset whose correct interpretation bears on positions tied to the perceiver's cultural or political identity, so that motivated interpretation can operate.
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from an experiment using a gun control ban framing; the thesis is offered as an account of culturally charged decision-relevant science, not of all quantitative reasoning, where numerate subjects did substantially better.
target_learners: general public members interpreting decision-relevant science
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of empirical data bearing on politically contested societal risks
examples: The article's experiment reframed one dataset as a gun control ban study, inducing polarization that grew with numeracy.
key_sources: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2

article_title: The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset
citation: Jiao Chen and Chunhui Liu. (2023). The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset. Front. Psychol. 14:1110944. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1110944
title: Identity control and intergenerational transmission accounts of how parental beliefs shape children's mindsets
description: The article frames parental influence on children's growth mindset through intergenerational transmission theory, in which parental characteristics pass to offspring via genes and environment, and identity control theory, under which children perceive others' attitudes, compare them with their own standards, and adjust. The article states that when children find that parents believe ability can change through effort, they internalize this belief, so "children’s perceived parental beliefs and behaviors can predict their mindset." This framework motivates testing mothers' and fathers' trajectories separately.
requirements: Parents and children must interact regularly so that children can perceive parental beliefs and behaviors during parenting
constraints: The article notes previous studies have not found a direct correlation between parents' mindset and children's mindset, so the framework's empirical support in this study is limited to the maternal paths found
target_learners: senior primary school children (grades 4–6)
target_learning_goals: children's beliefs about the malleability of ability (growth mindset)
examples: The study tested the framework with five-wave parallel process latent growth models separating fathers and mothers, finding support only for maternal paths
key_sources: Jiao Chen and Chunhui Liu. (2023). The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset. Front. Psychol. 14:1110944. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1110944

article_title: Knowledge building–modeling: Grade 5 students creating models, using discourse analytics, and advancing systems thinking
citation: Dina Soliman, Xueqi Feng, Marlene Scardamalia, Carol Chan. (2026). Knowledge building–modeling: Grade 5 students creating models, using discourse analytics, and advancing systems thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09493-8
title: Idea-Friend Maps: student-facing visualizations of discourse word networks derived from KBDeX
description: Idea-Friend Maps are a student-facing representation based on KBDeX word networks, preserving 'the semantic co-occurrence logic of KBDeX while presenting it in a more interpretable form for students'. Concepts that frequently co-occur in student notes are grouped and visually connected as 'friendships', and color-coded concept clusters help learners identify conceptual commonalities and cross-concept connections. Teachers use the visual cues to help students notice the state of community knowledge as a basis for reflection and improvement.
requirements: Generated from student Knowledge Forum discourse using KBDeX techniques, with researchers and teachers applying color codes to highlight key conceptual categories
constraints: Prior KBDeX applications 'have largely remained researcher-facing, with limited attention to use of its visualizations by students', which Idea-Friend Maps were developed to bridge
target_learners: elementary students (grade 5, ages 11–12)
target_learning_goals: reflecting on community knowledge
identifying conceptual gaps and planning model revisions
systems thinking
examples: In phase 2 of the unit, students used the Idea-Friend Map to engage in meta-discourse, examining clusters of ideas, identifying missing links such as between dynamic mechanisms and impacts, and planning model revisions
key_sources: Dina Soliman, Xueqi Feng, Marlene Scardamalia, Carol Chan. (2026). Knowledge building–modeling: Grade 5 students creating models, using discourse analytics, and advancing systems thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09493-8

article_title: The Effects of Group differentiation by students’ learning strategies
citation: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0
title: IDDI: Interactive Differentiated Directed Instruction model
description: The IDDI model is a variant of direct instruction extended with cooperative methods and convergent differentiation in groups. Lessons start with a common introduction, after which the instruction-independent group works independently while the teacher provides interactive group instruction to the rest, followed by prolonged instruction and guided practice for the instruction-dependent group. The article calls it "a variant of the direct instruction model that is found to be one of the most effective instruction methods."
requirements: Teachers trained in the model through two meetings, with additional expert support available during the intervention period
constraints: Implementation observations showed the difference between the middle and upper group was perhaps less clear than envisioned
target_learners: Secondary school students in heterogeneous classrooms
target_learning_goals: Subject-matter learning across mathematics, languages, and sciences
examples: Teachers performed the intervention minimally once a week for eight months, developing or finding materials with the option to submit them to an expert for advice
key_sources: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0

article_title: The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis
citation: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2
title: Idiodynamic method for capturing micro-level emotion dynamics in language use
description: The idiodynamic method tracks moment-to-moment changes in subjective emotional intensity during communication events. Operationally, "the idiodynamic method relies on post hoc recalling of language behaviours stimulated by according video": participants review recordings of short communication episodes and continuously rate target factors by pressing buttons indicating increases or decreases, with ratings returning to a neutral value when no button is pressed. The review reports it has revealed that anxiety and enjoyment levels can vary significantly within a single task or interaction, but that correlation-based analyses still yield largely static results.
requirements: Specialized software facilitating granular analysis of communication events, and video recordings of the communication episodes for post hoc review
constraints: The button-clicking and value-returning mechanism may introduce task switching and multitasking that could promote anxiety and affect cognitive load and working memory, interfering with the natural cognitive processes of language use
The only available idiodynamic software has limited compatibility with high-resolution tools like EEG, restricting concurrent capture of subjective and physiological data
target_learners: Second language learners in communication tasks
target_learning_goals: Capturing real-time fluctuations of emotions such as anxiety and enjoyment during language use
examples: The review cites studies applying the method to SLA factors, finding that anxiety and enjoyment levels can vary significantly within a single task or interaction
key_sources: Peng Wang, Lesya Ganushchak, Camille Welie, Roel van Steensel. (2024). The Dynamic Nature of Emotions in Language Learning Context: Theory, Method, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09946-2

article_title: Linguistic precursors of sixth-grade geometric and fraction skills in children with and without Developmental Language Disorder
citation: Kleemans, T., Vissers, C. T. W. M., & Segers, E. (2025). Linguistic precursors of sixth-grade geometric and fraction skills in children with and without Developmental Language Disorder. Learning and Instruction, 95, 102019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102019
title: Identify individual cognitive strengths and integrate them into standardized test batteries and treatment approaches for children with DLD
description: The article argues that because children with DLD are highly heterogeneous, compensatory strengths may only appear at the individual level, so "identifying individual strengths should be integrated into standardized test batteries and treatment approaches." The case-series analysis showed a verbal-reasoning strength brought DLD children's geometry and fraction scores into the normal range, so assessment should profile strengths rather than only deficits.
requirements: Individual-level (case-series) analysis in addition to group comparisons, because group-level analyses did not identify specific strengths for children with DLD
constraints: The DLD sample attended Dutch special education, so generalization to children with DLD in mainstream education was not supported by the study
target_learners: Upper-primary-grade children with Developmental Language Disorder
target_learning_goals: Geometric skills
Fraction skills
examples: The study defined strengths as scores 1 SD above the TD-group mean and used a follow-up MANCOVA to show DLD children with a verbal-reasoning strength scored within the average range on geometry and fractions
key_sources: Kleemans, T., Vissers, C. T. W. M., & Segers, E. (2025). Linguistic precursors of sixth-grade geometric and fraction skills in children with and without Developmental Language Disorder. Learning and Instruction, 95, 102019. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102019

article_title: School belonging predicts whether an emerging adult will be not in education, employment, or training (NEET) after school.
citation: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). School Belonging Predicts whether an Emerging Adult will be Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET) after School. https://www.pwc.com.au/government/government-matters/youth-unemployment.html
title: Identity capital and the politics of belonging as an explanatory framework linking school belonging to NEET
description: The article frames school belonging and NEET via two sociological theories. Identity capital is "the tangible (connections, ways of speaking, memberships of a group, and ways of dressing) and intangible (self-belief, self-regulatory skills...) resources that provide access to opportunities". The politics of belonging examines how "social positions and identities are diﬀerentially valued and contested" and how community boundaries determine who belongs. Low school belonging may signal low identity capital, which then disadvantages youth in labor-market and tertiary 'identity markets', making belonging a psychological precursor to wider institutional exclusion.
requirements: The framework assumes youth identities must compete in institutional 'identity markets' of school, labor market, and tertiary education
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical interpretation of the belonging-NEET link, not a tested mechanism; other mechanisms such as social exclusion experience and mental-health costs are flagged for future research
target_learners: secondary school students approaching the post-compulsory transition
target_learning_goals: social inclusion and belonging at school
successful transition to further education, employment, or training
examples: The study tested whether belonging's effect operated through high-school graduation and found it did not, leaving identity-based mechanisms as candidate explanations
key_sources: Philip Parker, Kelly-Ann Allen, Rhiannon Parker, Jiesi Guo, Herbert W Marsh, Geetanjali Basarkod, and Theresa Dicke. (2021). School Belonging Predicts whether an Emerging Adult will be Not in Education, Employment, or Training (NEET) after School. https://www.pwc.com.au/government/government-matters/youth-unemployment.html

article_title: Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components
citation: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y
title: IDyOM information content as a note-by-note measure of temporal predictability in rhythms
description: The Information Dynamics of Music (IDyOM) model is a computational model that captures statistical features of music; in this study it quantifies the temporal predictability of each individual note. The article states that "Information content (IC) gives a quantitative measure of the unpredictability of an event based on extracting the statistical properties of a corpus of music by which the model is trained." The model was trained on 185 chorale melodies by Bach, using onset, inter-onset interval and metrical accent viewpoints, and the authors note it "tries to simulate the process of musical enculturation and statistical learning of musical features of humans".
requirements: A predefined training corpus from which onset, inter-onset interval and metric accent probabilities are extracted
constraints: IC reflects statistics of the training corpus and the experimental rhythms; in this study the corpus was 185 Bach chorale melodies
target_learners: adult non-musicians learning rhythmic sequences
target_learning_goals: temporal prediction and accurate timing of rhythmic production
examples: The nine experimental rhythms were selected according to their information content (Table 1 reports mean, SD, min and max IC per rhythm)
key_sources: Marc Deosdad-Díez & Josep Marco-Pallarés. (2025). Note-by-note predictability modulates rhythm learning and its neural components. npj Science of Learning 10:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00353-y

article_title: What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning
citation: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5
title: Determine what you want to know and how it relates to design before identifying which learning data are needed
description: The commentary recommends that before collecting analytics, practitioners determine what they want to know, what is already known, and how this relates to design; only then can the needed data be identified. It stresses that "Identifying the right data is crucial to getting learning analytics right", noting some data are easy to access, some unavailable, and some available but not useful. Both big data and small data about individuals and particular tasks matter.
requirements: Explicit determination of the questions to be answered and their relation to learning design before data collection
constraints: Some needed data may not be available, and some available data are not useful, as the article states
target_learners: students in online and blended learning environments across education levels
target_learning_goals: monitoring and supporting student learning through appropriately chosen data
examples: The article contrasts mass collection of behavioural data with the need for small data about individuals and particular learning tasks
key_sources: Jason M. Lodge and Linda Corrin. (2017). What data and analytics can and do say about effective learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0006-5

article_title: Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations
citation: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9
title: Identify students' knowledge profiles, including decay functions, before proposing curriculum customization
description: Because the student profile strongly affects solving FIC/DK-P, institutions should assess not only current mastery but how each student forgets before individualizing curricula. The authors recommend that "institutions must therefore be careful to identify the precise profile of their students before proposing customization," warning that otherwise the risk is "to propose sequences of courses irrelevant to students' needs."
requirements: Regular assessment instruments capable of estimating and refining per-student decay functions over the years.
constraints: Cluster-based assignment of predefined decay functions is described as possibly less efficient than individual self-positioning testing.
target_learners: students entering individualized curriculum tracks at universities and engineering schools
target_learning_goals: accurate prediction of knowledge decay to keep personalized curricula relevant to student needs
examples: The authors propose conducting self-positioning tests to regularly test and compare the evolution of students' knowledge, or clustering students by features such as grades and high school specialties and assigning predefined decay functions.
key_sources: Lebis, A., Humeau, J., Fleury, A., Lucas, F., & Vermeulen, M. (2024). Fully Individualized Curriculum with Decaying Knowledge, a New Hard Problem: Investigation and Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00376-9

article_title: Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education
citation: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0
title: Hong and Sullivan's idea-centered discourse framework: sharing-, argument-, and integration-oriented discourse
description: The article applies Hong and Sullivan's (2009) framework for sustained idea improvement, which "proposes three idea-centered discourse processes: idea-generation/diversification (sharing-oriented discourse), idea-argumentation/justification (argument-oriented discourse), and idea-integration/synthesis (integration-oriented discourse)". The study used this framework as the coding scheme for discourse moves and as the pedagogical structure for cultivating sense of promisingness in thesis-proposal development.
requirements: Discourse moves coded from connected note pairs (a note and its build-on note) in Knowledge Forum
target_learners: graduate students developing thesis proposals
target_learning_goals: judging promising thesis ideas
sustained idea improvement through discourse
key_sources: Huang-Yao Hong, Mei-Ju Chen, Bodong Chen, Chao-Yu Guo, Li-Ting Tseng (2025). Sense of promisingness: towards creative expertise through knowledge-building discourse in online graduate education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10483-0

article_title: What does it mean to be “career ready”? A study of competencies important for instructional designers and educational technologists
citation: Exter, M., & Ashby, I. (2026). What does it mean to be “career ready”? A study of competencies important for instructional designers and educational technologists. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10727-7
title: Taxonomy of ID/ET professional competencies spanning domain knowledge and skills, cross-disciplinary skills, and dispositions
description: The article presents a taxonomy of professional competencies for instructional design and educational technology roles, organized into three themes: domain knowledge and skills, professional/cross-disciplinary skills, and dispositions. Each theme is broken into sub-themes and categories, with frequency counts by role and context. The authors state they “decided to combine knowledge and skills, and break up into two logical themes: “domain knowledge & skills” and “cross-disciplinary knowledge and skills””, with dispositions as a separate theme.
requirements: Competency definitions must be grounded in what professionals report as important on the job, using an operational definition of ID and ET roles to determine inclusion.
constraints: The taxonomy reflects competencies reported by 31 professionals across K12, higher education, and corporate contexts; it is not a validated universal standard.
target_learners: Instructional design and educational technology professionals
Current and future ID/ET graduate students
target_learning_goals: Career readiness
Professional competency development
key_sources: Exter, M., & Ashby, I. (2026). What does it mean to be “career ready”? A study of competencies important for instructional designers and educational technologists. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10727-7

article_title: Effect of mental hygiene films on normal and abnormal individuals
citation: Stein, Elisabeth Mays. (1955). Effect of Mental Hygiene Films on Normal and Abnormal Individuals. Technical Report SDC 269-7-46, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University.
title: Identification-relevance account of learning from mental-health films
description: The article's findings organize around viewer identification and perceived relevance as the mechanisms linking film viewing to learning and self-disclosure about mental health. Viewers differ in identification by psychological status and sex, and identification relates to talking about personal problems, suggesting relevance and acceptability as central conditions for film-based mental-health instruction.
requirements: Films must be relevant and acceptable to the target audience.
constraints: Findings reported for normal college students and acutely ill or deviant individuals; generalization beyond these groups is not established.
target_learners: college students
psychiatric patients
target_learning_goals: mental health attitudes and knowledge
key_sources: Stein, Elisabeth Mays. (1955). Effect of Mental Hygiene Films on Normal and Abnormal Individuals. Technical Report SDC 269-7-46, Instructional Film Research Program, Pennsylvania State University. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02719932

article_title: Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography
citation: Fiock, H., Meech, S., Yang, M., Long, Y., Farmer, T., Hilliard, N., Koehler, A. A., & Cheng, Z. (2022). Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10075-8
title: Sensemaking approaches to theoretical understanding in instructional design
description: The article organizes its findings around a framework of sensemaking approaches ID learners use: deconstructing theory, distinguishing terminology, integrating concepts with previous knowledge, maintaining openness to multiple perspectives, personalizing understanding, and applying theory. The authors describe how learners move from basic, perfunctory understanding through awareness of insufficient knowledge toward constructed understanding, with struggle as an integral emotional and intellectual component. The framework draws on Weick et al.'s (2005) sensemaking concept and Meyer and Land's (2006) threshold concepts and liminality.
requirements: Learners must encounter complex, abstract theory with inconsistent terminology to trigger the sensemaking process
constraints: Findings stem from a single collaborative autoethnography of six learners in one course and may not generalize to other settings
target_learners: instructional design doctoral students
novice instructional designers
target_learning_goals: developing deep theoretical understanding of ID theory
key_sources: Fiock, H., Meech, S., Yang, M., Long, Y., Farmer, T., Hilliard, N., Koehler, A. A., & Cheng, Z. (2022). Instructional design learners make sense of theory: a collaborative autoethnography. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10075-8

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students
citation: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8
title: Individual digital study assistants (IDSA) as online student support tools that strengthen self-regulation, goal achievement, and study organization
description: The article defines an IDSA as "an efficient online student support tool that strengthens self-regulation skills, goal achievement, and study organization through suitable functionalities". Unlike pedagogical conversational agents, an IDSA does not directly assist in learning content; instead it provides individual study structuring, situation-specific guidance, and recommendations based on individual goals, interests, and competencies. It accesses information from student dialogs, campus and learning management systems, completed modules, and external resources such as OER platforms.
requirements: Must access information sources including student-provided details, campus and learning management system data, and external resources such as OER platforms to generate individualized support and recommendations
constraints: Contrary to a pedagogical conversational agent, an IDSA is not directly involved in the different facets of the learning process and handles learning content only on a reflective level
target_learners: Higher education students in their early study phase
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning
study organization
goal setting and achievement
key_sources: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8

article_title: Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students
citation: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8
title: Multi-functionality in a digital study assistant must not come at the expense of the depth and content of individual functionalities
description: Drawing on the field-test feedback that functionalities were rated only slightly above the satisfaction level and that students "only perceived limited added value from certain functionalities", the article advises that "Multi-functionality must not be achieved at the expense of the depth and content of individual functionalities". It further suggests the need to critically evaluate an IDSA prototype's maturity before its deployment, and that functionalities can be individually adapted to address student groups within different life cycle phases.
requirements: An intensive test phase with student feedback incorporation before rollout, so weaknesses are identified and corrected
constraints: Usability and user-friendliness may be limited when the assistant is integrated into an existing learning management or campus management system that predefines frontend structure and navigation
target_learners: Higher education students, particularly those in their early study phase
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning, study organization, and goal achievement through digital study support
examples: The prototype offered eight functionalities including To-do, Personality, Organization of Learning, Get-Together, OER, Interests, Evaluation, and Data Sovereignty, and was field-tested for three months in three German higher education institutions
key_sources: Karrenbauer, C., Brauner, T., König, C. M., & Breitner, M. H. (2023). Design, development, and evaluation of an individual digital study assistant for higher education students. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10255-8

article_title: Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university
citation: Folabit, N. L., & Jita, L. C. (2026). Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10708-w
title: Integrated identity theory and TPACK framework for analysing teacher identity reconstruction in technology integration
description: The article integrates Stryker and Burke's identity theory with the TPACK framework as a combined analytical lens. Identity theory explains how academics interpret and negotiate roles through "role salience, role conflict, and identity tension," while TPACK explains how these processes are enacted through technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. The authors state identity theory "foregrounds the dynamics of self-reconstruction, and TPACK illustrates the pedagogical mechanism through which academics’ reconstruction of their teacher identity is materialised."
requirements: Analysts must map inductive codes to TPACK constructs (TK, PK, CK) and identity theory constructs (role identity, salience, conflict) to keep analysis conceptually coherent
constraints: The article notes TPACK does not fully address socio-structural challenges academics face, such as workload and infrastructure limitations
target_learners: University academics integrating technology into teaching
target_learning_goals: Professional identity reconstruction
Technology-integrated pedagogical practice
examples: The study applied the integrated framework in hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis of interviews with 12 academics, coding gamification and multimedia use under TPK and role conflict under identity reconstruction
key_sources: Folabit, N. L., & Jita, L. C. (2026). Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10708-w

article_title: Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment
citation: Noroozi, O., Busstra, M. C., Mulder, M., Biemans, H. J. A., Tobi, H., Geelen, A., van't Veer, P., Chizari, M. (2012). Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev (2012) 60:193-221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9217-2
title: IDLM platform and Drewlite CSCL platform with graphical knowledge maps
description: Two platforms carried the study's two learning tasks. The IDLM platform 'comprised a sequence of interactive exercises alternated with explanatory information such as texts, interactive diagrams, animations, video clips and schemes,' with drag-and-drop exercises, multiple choice questions, and detailed feedback on incorrect and correct answers. The CSCL platform Drewlite, a simplified version of Drew developed within the Scale project, 'comprises different tools for communication, collaboration, and argumentation such as chat, graph, text board, view board, and multi modules.' Its graph module let students build box-and-arrow knowledge maps with comment fields for tests 1 and 2, and its chat module supported the online discussion condition.
requirements: Teaching assistants were available to support technical difficulties, language issues, and progress monitoring
constraints: Drewlite is less elaborate in managing sessions and traces than the full Drew platform, which the authors judged irrelevant for their study
target_learners: third-year bachelor and first-year master students in Nutrition and Health
target_learning_goals: designing, analyzing and interpreting evaluation studies of nutritional assessment methods
examples: Students individually designed an evaluation study of a 24-h recall method over three 4-h sessions in IDLM, then discussed their test 1 knowledge maps in pairs for 90 minutes in Drewlite
key_sources: Noroozi, O., Busstra, M. C., Mulder, M., Biemans, H. J. A., Tobi, H., Geelen, A., van't Veer, P., Chizari, M. (2012). Online discussion compensates for suboptimal timing of supportive information presentation in a digitally supported learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev (2012) 60:193-221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-011-9217-2

article_title: NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods
citation: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4
title: Instructional design model for product development structured as 11 measurable modules across four design phases
description: The article proposes a prescriptive instructional design model for the Product Development Process, built on the design phases of Pahl et al. and split so each phase can be measured with NASA-TLX. The authors state: "We divide the design method into 11 modules to represent all the phases of product creation", with each module containing a minimum of three measurable activities. The four phases are clarification of the task, conceptual design, design embodiment, and detailed design and final product, spanning activities from data collection and sketching through CAD modelling to prototype manufacture and validation.
requirements: Design phases must be split into modules with specific, measurable tasks so NASA-TLX can be applied to each activity
constraints: The initial design methods need modification to have clear tasks measurable in practice; instructional design methods must have specific outcomes to be measurable and predictable
target_learners: young designers (design students/novice practitioners)
target_learning_goals: understanding and executing the product development design process phases
examples: In the case study, four young designers followed the 11 modules over more than 40 working hours to create a working surface attachable to a wheelchair, validated with handicapped teenagers from TELETON
key_sources: Christopher Nikulin, Gabriela Lopez, Eduardo Piñonez, Luis Gonzalez, Pia Zapata. (2019). NASA-TLX for predictability and measurability of instructional design models: case study in design methods. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09657-4

article_title: Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness
citation: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229
title: Ideation Hub online brainstorming platform
description: The Ideation Hub is an online platform built for this study to run structured hybrid brainstorming sessions. It "provides task instructions for both individual and group phases, enforces time limits, and presents the necessary rules before and during each phase". It delivers condition-specific scaffolds: SCAMPER question prompts with principle descriptions and examples in the experimental conditions, and condition-dependent display or hiding of individually generated ideas during the group phase to manipulate cognitive group awareness.
requirements: An online platform able to deliver timed phase instructions, display prompts, and control visibility of individually generated ideas across group members
constraints: The platform was designed specifically for this study and its scaffolds were implemented for a business-idea generation task on sustainable development
target_learners: higher education students, mostly master's level, in agriculture and food sciences programs
target_learning_goals: generating original business ideas addressing sustainability issues through divergent thinking
examples: In experimental 1 and 2 conditions participants could view their previously generated ideas and were encouraged to apply SCAMPER principles using built-in question prompts with a description and example of each principle
key_sources: Farrokhnia, M., Noroozi, O., Baggen, Y., Biemans, H., & Weinberger, A. (2024). Improving hybrid brainstorming outcomes with computer-supported scaffolds: Prompts and cognitive group awareness. Computers & Education 227 (2025) 105229. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105229

article_title: Educators' open educational collaboration online: The dilemma of emotional ownership
citation: Educators' Open Educational Collaboration Online: The Dilemma of Emotional Ownership. (2016). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115784
title: Idea-sharing platform for collaborative development of educational ideas
description: The study used an online platform dedicated to idea sharing for new OER and courses, supporting collaborative OER development between interested peers. It supports both closed collaboration and fully open, transparent sharing that allows anyone to join, which enabled the researchers to study differences between open and closed knowledge exchange. Platform descriptives for January 2015 to January 2016 report 466 registered users, 118 workspaces created (88 active), and contributions ranging from 1-103 per workspace.
requirements: Users must be able to form both closed workspaces with known peers and fully open workspaces
constraints: Commenting on posts was not counted as a contribution due to notification overload for users
target_learners: educators using or developing OER
target_learning_goals: collaborative ideation and development of open educational resources
key_sources: Educators' Open Educational Collaboration Online: The Dilemma of Emotional Ownership. (2016). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115784

article_title: IDR: A participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning
citation: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043
title: IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary techno-pedagogical design
description: IDR is a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary techno-pedagogical design in technology enhanced learning. It draws on the design patterns tradition and the design research paradigm, and was developed iteratively by a pan-European project team of educational researchers, software developers and teachers. The article presents it as a response to design processes that 'often lack true interdisciplinarity' despite the multi-dimensional nature of designing technology for learning.
requirements: Participation of educational researchers, software developers and teachers in the design process
target_learners: designers of technology enhanced learning
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary design of learning technologies
key_sources: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043

article_title: IDR: A participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning
citation: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043
title: Open source web toolkit for collaborative design pattern creation
description: The article reports that a distributed pan-European project team developed 'a set of over 120 design patterns, created using our freely available open source web toolkit'. The toolkit supports the participatory, collaborative creation of design patterns by interdisciplinary teams working at a distance. It is described as freely available and open source.
requirements: Access to the freely available open source web toolkit
target_learners: educational researchers
software developers
teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative design pattern creation
key_sources: Niall Winters, Yishay Mor. (2007). IDR: a participatory methodology for interdisciplinary design in technology enhanced learning. Computers and Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190043

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Reading and Writing Interventions for Students with Disorders of Intellectual Development
citation: Bakken, R.K.; Næss, K.-A.B.; Lemons, C.J.; Hjetland, H.N. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Reading and Writing Interventions for Students with Disorders of Intellectual Development. Educ. Sci. 2021, 11, 638. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11100638
title: Effective reading interventions for students with disorders of ID combine phonics-based decoding (often with sight-word instruction), linguistic comprehension, and supplemental instruction adapted to adaptive and cognitive challenges
description: Across the nine included studies, reading programmes were phonics-based and frequently combined decoding with sight-word reading: "Five studies combined decoding with sight-word instructions". Targeted decoding skills included sound blending and segmentation, word recognition, text reading, fluency, and single word reading. Most interventions also included linguistic comprehension instruction, and almost all used supplemental strategies addressing adaptive and cognitive challenges such as explicit instruction, time delays, reinforcement, repeated practice, short sessions, and behaviour management.
requirements: Interventions must be adapted to participants' adaptive and cognitive skills, e.g., via explicit instruction, systematic prompting, and repeated practice opportunities
constraints: The review tested multifaceted interventions rather than individual content components, so the contribution of each component is unknown
target_learners: Students aged 4–19 with disorders of intellectual development (mild-to-moderate IQ range 41.5–58.4 in the included studies)
target_learning_goals: Word reading and decoding of taught and untrained words
Linguistic comprehension
examples: Browder et al. developed the Early Literacy Skills Builder adapted for AAC users; Burgoyne et al. combined phonics, text reading and sight-word instruction with games and graded books for students with Down syndrome
key_sources: Bakken, R.K.; Næss, K.-A.B.; Lemons, C.J.; Hjetland, H.N. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Reading and Writing Interventions for Students with Disorders of Intellectual Development. Educ. Sci. 2021, 11, 638. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11100638

article_title: An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education
citation: Katharina Spintzyk, Friederike Strehlke, Stephanie Ohlberger, Bernd Gröben, and Claas Wegner. (2016). An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education. Science Educator, Vol. 25, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=An+Empirical+Study+Investigating+Interdisciplinary+Teaching+of+Biology+and+Physical+Education
title: Pre-/post knowledge test on interdisciplinary biology–PE content
description: A knowledge test and detailed evaluation sheet were developed to examine IdT's effectiveness regarding students' growth in knowledge. The pre-post-test includes closed, semi-open and open questions so foreknowledge and performance development could be compared, with a detailed level of expectations and double proofreading for objectivity. "The knowledge test's reliability amounted to Cronbach's alpha of α = 0.710 at the time of measure- ment t2", and separation efficiency of the questions achieved results of >0.2. The test was piloted with 23 pupils and adjusted for reliability and selectivity.
requirements: Students were expected to reproduce new knowledge and transfer newly learned content to novel tasks
constraints: Reliability was measured only at t2; t1 served to check pre-knowledge, and the authors state reliability should be improved in follow-up work
target_learners: German grammar school students in fifth and sixth form
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of human biology and endurance training content
Application of newly learned content to novel tasks
examples: Figure 1 provides example closed, semi-open and open task questions from the pre-post-test
key_sources: Katharina Spintzyk, Friederike Strehlke, Stephanie Ohlberger, Bernd Gröben, and Claas Wegner. (2016). An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education. Science Educator, Vol. 25, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110252

article_title: Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reverse Transfer of Reading Strategies
citation: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217
title: Graduated scaffolding of strategy instruction through I do it, We do it, You do it phases
description: The intervention scaffolded strategy learning in three stages: "I do it, in which the teacher models the strategy by thinking aloud for students", a We do it stage of cooperative group practice with teacher support, and a You do it stage in which students apply strategies more independently with supportive scaffolding. This operationalised the principle that the teacher gradually removes supports so students can practice independently, within the Scaffolding Reading Experience planning and implementation phases.
requirements: Teacher modeling via think-aloud in the first phase
Cooperative groups with defined roles in the second phase
Independent reading tasks with supportive scaffolding in the third phase
constraints: The course consisted of sixteen sessions of 70 minutes delivered by the researcher within normal class hours
target_learners: Intermediate and advanced secondary EFL readers
target_learning_goals: Independent strategic reading
Transfer of strategies across texts and tasks
examples: After teacher modeling, students formed groups of five and collaboratively implemented preview, click and clunk, get the gist, and wrap-up before individual practice
key_sources: Seyed Hassan Talebi. (2012). Reading in L2 (English) and L1 (Persian): An Investigation into Reveres Transfer of Reading Strategies. English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n3p217

article_title: An Investigation of the Possible Effects of Favored Contexts in Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Omid Rezaei, Salman Dezhara. (2011). An Investigation of the Possible Effects of Favored Contexts in Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p97
title: Identify learners' needs, preferences and interest areas before designing reading materials for vocabulary learning
description: The article recommends that material designers take learners' interests into account when preparing reading passages and activities for vocabulary teaching. It states: "It is suggested that students' needs, preferences and interest areas be identified prior to designing the intended material, specially reading passages and activities." In this study that was done via a pre-study questionnaire in which 41 students named their most and least preferred topics.
requirements: A means of identifying learners' needs, preferences and interest areas, such as the topic-preference questionnaire used in this study, before materials are designed
constraints: The article also cautions that "not a universal prescription can be provided for all contexts and teaching and learning situations", and its own favored-topic result did not show a vocabulary-learning advantage for the favored topic
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners in language institutes
target_learning_goals: Second language vocabulary acquisition through reading
examples: The researchers gave 41 students a questionnaire asking which of four subject matters they would like most and which they would dislike, then built treatment passages on sport (favored) and geography (disfavored)
key_sources: Omid Rezaei, Salman Dezhara. (2011). An Investigation of the Possible Effects of Favored Contexts in Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p97

article_title: Academic Resilience in Contexts of Inequality: Motivational and Self-Efficacy Profiles of Disadvantaged High Achievers.
citation: Rémeau Margot, Raffy Gaël, Borst Grégoire. (2026). Academic Resilience in Contexts of Inequality: Motivational and Self‐Efficacy Profiles of Disadvantaged High Achievers. Journal of Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1002/jad.70190
title: Motivational vulnerabilities should be identified and supported across the full socioeconomic spectrum, moving beyond SES as a sole marker of risk
description: The article found that low‐achieving students from higher‐SES backgrounds consistently reported lower levels of self‐efficacy and intrinsic motivation, which may partly account for their underachievement. The article argues these findings "underscore the importance of identifying and supporting motivational vulnerabilities across the full socioeconomic spectrum and argue for differentiated intervention strategies that move beyond SES as a sole marker of risk."
requirements: Assessment of motivational resources should not be limited to students identified as socioeconomically disadvantaged
constraints: The article notes that socioeconomic advantage alone does not guarantee strong motivational resources
target_learners: Early adolescents across all socioeconomic backgrounds in lower secondary education
target_learning_goals: Academic self‐efficacy
Intrinsic motivation
Academic achievement
examples: Low‐achieving students from higher‐SES backgrounds consistently reported lower levels of self‐efficacy and intrinsic motivation in the French panel data
key_sources: Rémeau Margot, Raffy Gaël, Borst Grégoire. (2026). Academic Resilience in Contexts of Inequality: Motivational and Self‐Efficacy Profiles of Disadvantaged High Achievers. Journal of Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1002/jad.70190

article_title: Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates' knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus.
citation: Mariam S, Heba I, Mohamed FHN. (2025). Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates’ knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06602-9
title: Use a 'don't know' option on assessments to separate knowledge gaps from guessing
description: The article's MCQs included “one correct answer, 3 distractors and one ‘I don’t know’ option to mitigate forced guessing”; these responses were excluded from scores and analysed separately as a measure of self-awareness. This design choice is what allowed the authors to detect that game-group students more often admitted uncertainty while control students more often guessed incorrectly. It supports assessing metacognitive accuracy alongside accuracy.
requirements: Assessment items must include a non-scored 'I don't know' option, and its frequency must be analysed separately from scored responses
constraints: The study excluded 'I don't know' responses from score calculations, so knowledge scores reflect only correct/incorrect choices
target_learners: Preclinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing genuine knowledge from guessed answers; recognizing the limits of one's knowledge
examples: The 10 pre/post MCQs each carried the option, and its post-test frequency differed significantly between the game and self-study groups
key_sources: Mariam S, Heba I, Mohamed FHN. (2025). Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates’ knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06602-9

article_title: Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency - impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes.
citation: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/
title: Immune Deficiency Foundation (IDF) patient survey on SCIG training, infusion characteristics, and patient-reported outcomes
description: The Immune Deficiency Foundation conducted an online survey of US-based patients with primary immunodeficiency (or their parent/caregiver if under 18) regarding SCIG training and infusion experiences. Using the IDF patient database, 11,232 patients were contacted regarding an unincentivized online survey containing 74 questions, including the TSQM, PROMIS Fatigue SF7a/SF10, and GHP measures. In total, 35.3% (366/1037) of responders were included in the analyses, with adult patients accounting for 89% (n = 326) and parent/caregiver proxy responses for patients under 18 accounting for 11% (n = 40).
requirements: Respondents currently receiving SCIG treatment
Complete and congruent survey responses
constraints: As a non-probability sample, generalization of results to the larger population should be made with caution
Responses could not be independently verified with patients' physicians
target_learners: US-based patients with primary immunodeficiency on SCIG treatment
Parent/caregiver proxy respondents for pediatric patients
target_learning_goals: Assessing patient-reported outcomes in relation to SCIG training and infusion characteristics
examples: The survey assessed training characteristics including location, who conducted training, number of sessions, session length, trainer competence and knowledge, ease of training, confidence after training, and barriers to training
key_sources: Mallick R., Henderson T., Lahue B. J., Kafal A., Bassett P., Scalchunes C. (2020). Subcutaneous immunoglobulin in primary immunodeficiency – impact of training and infusion characteristics on patient-reported outcomes. BMC Immunology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7418302/

article_title: Comparison of surgical skill acquisition by UK surgical trainees and Sierra Leonean associate clinicians in a task-sharing programme.
citation: Liu B., Hunt L. M., Lonsdale R. J., Narula H. S., Mansaray A. F., Bundu I. and Bolkan H. A. (2019). Comparison of surgical skill acquisition by UK surgical trainees and Sierra Leonean associate clinicians in a task‐sharing programme. BJS Open 3(2): 218–223. https://doi.org/10.1002/bjs5.50122
title: Train non-medically qualified surgical providers with identical training and expectations to medically qualified trainees, because equal or superior skill acquisition can result
description: The article's central design recommendation is that associate clinicians in surgical task-sharing programmes should receive the same training, in the same time, as medically qualified trainees, since the study found that "with identical training, Sierra Leonean community health officers showed equal or superior skill acquisition, greater confidence and better communication than UK surgical trainees". It further argues that "failure to recognize their abilities is a barrier to their successful deployment and retention", so training and deployment should not assume inferior capability.
requirements: Identical training materials and practice time across trainee groups
Assessment with validated tools to demonstrate competence objectively
constraints: Evidence comes from a single simulated procedure (venous cut-down); the article notes limitations regarding more complex procedures and real-life surgery
The UK group had significantly more surgical experience, an unintended imbalance the authors acknowledge
target_learners: associate clinicians in surgical task-sharing programmes
surgical trainees in early years of training
target_learning_goals: essential and emergency surgical and obstetric skills
competence equal to medically qualified trainees within the same training time
examples: A 2-year surgical task-sharing programme in Sierra Leone enrolled predominantly community health officers and added a designated basic surgical skills course in 2014
key_sources: Liu B., Hunt L. M., Lonsdale R. J., Narula H. S., Mansaray A. F., Bundu I. and Bolkan H. A. (2019). Comparison of surgical skill acquisition by UK surgical trainees and Sierra Leonean associate clinicians in a task‐sharing programme. BJS Open 3(2): 218–223. https://doi.org/10.1002/bjs5.50122

article_title: Intellectual disability content within tertiary medical curriculum: how is it taught and by whom?
citation: Trollor JN, Eagleson C, Turner B, Tracy J, Torr JJ, Durvasula S, Iacono T, Cvejic RC, Lennox N. (2018). Intellectual disability content within tertiary medical curriculum: how is it taught and by whom? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1286-z
title: Medical schools should renew intellectual disability curricula using varied teaching methods and inclusive teaching involving people with intellectual disability
description: The authors urge schools to review how they teach intellectual disability health and to adopt varied methods that support self-directed learning, practical experience and inclusive teaching. They argue diverse delivery, such as workshops, clinic visits and placements, better develops skills and attitudes than reliance on didactic lectures, and that inclusive teaching "provides a powerful approach for changing attitudes and perceptions". The recommendation follows directly from the audit's finding of heavy lecture use and inconsistent inclusive involvement.
requirements: Teaching methods should match stated learning objectives, with knowledge, skills and attitudes each addressed by appropriate methods
Inclusive teaching requires involving people with intellectual disability in developing or providing education
constraints: The audit found schools face competing demands for curriculum space in medical degree courses
Assessment of the content is needed for motivation and retention; unassessed content risks not being retained over the long term
target_learners: medical students in Australian medical schools
target_learning_goals: knowledge, skills, attitudes and confidence in intellectual disability health
adapting clinical practice for people with intellectual disability
examples: The authors state: "we urge medical schools to evaluate how they teach medical students about intellectual disability health, and take steps to incorporate varied methods that encourage self-directed learning, practical experience, and inclusive teaching"
key_sources: Trollor JN, Eagleson C, Turner B, Tracy J, Torr JJ, Durvasula S, Iacono T, Cvejic RC, Lennox N. (2018). Intellectual disability content within tertiary medical curriculum: how is it taught and by whom? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1286-z

article_title: Antimicrobial knowledge and confidence amongst final year medical students in Australia.
citation: Weier N, Thursky K, Zaidi STR. (2017). Antimicrobial knowledge and confidence amongst final year medical students in Australia. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0182460
title: Validated survey tool for medical students' infectious diseases knowledge, confidence, and education perceptions
description: A six-section online survey covering demographics, formal education and training, confidence in antibiotic prescribing, knowledge and attitudes towards antimicrobial prescribing guidelines, perceptions of antimicrobial resistance, and clinical knowledge cases. The article states it is "a survey tool with demonstrated reliability and validity", with Cronbach's alpha >0.7 obtained for the main sections. It is the tool the authors developed because "there currently is no reliable survey tool available in the literature for this subject matter".
requirements: Reliability analysis with Cronbach's alpha and Pearson correlation for criterion-related validity, as the article reports performing
constraints: The section on perceptions of antibiotic resistance showed variable reliability if certain questions were not included; the authors suggest removing one question could improve reliability in further studies
target_learners: final-year medical students
target_learning_goals: infectious diseases knowledge and antimicrobial prescribing confidence
examples: Used in an eight-week online survey of final-year medical students across Australian universities in August–September 2015, yielding 191 responses with 163 analysed
key_sources: Weier N, Thursky K, Zaidi STR. (2017). Antimicrobial knowledge and confidence amongst final year medical students in Australia. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0182460

article_title: "For most of us Africans, we don't just speak": a qualitative investigation into collaborative heterogeneous PBL group learning.
citation: Singaram Veena S., van der Vleuten Cees P. M., Stevens Fred, Dolmans Diana H. J. M. (2010). “For most of us Africans, we don’t just speak”: a qualitative investigation into collaborative heterogeneous PBL group learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-010-9262-3
title: Collaborative heterogeneous group learning as a scale balancing the 'ideology' and the 'practice' of mixing diverse students
description: The study's central framework portrays collaborative heterogeneous PBL group learning "as a scale": on one side the 'ideology' behind mixing diverse students with its positive advantages, on the other the 'practice' behind mixing students with its negative side. The authors link this to earlier characterizations of diversity as a double-edged sword. Three balancing dilemmas structure the findings: interaction versus segregation, professional preparation versus status inequity, and mutual learning versus learning hindered by language and academic differences.
requirements: Balancing the scale requires the three recommendations: active facilitation, teacher training, and the right mix
constraints: The framework derives from a single-site qualitative focus group study at one South African medical school; the authors call for more research in other countries and cultures
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in diverse PBL groups
target_learning_goals: understanding diversity's dual effects on collaborative group learning
examples: The conclusion states the scale "appears to be tipped to the positive end" because the challenges can be addressed
key_sources: Singaram Veena S., van der Vleuten Cees P. M., Stevens Fred, Dolmans Diana H. J. M. (2010). “For most of us Africans, we don’t just speak”: a qualitative investigation into collaborative heterogeneous PBL group learning. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-010-9262-3
